units.t: First Aid Basics by Ear.
Part one. Before you start.
Imagine you're at the shops, and a man a few metres away suddenly collapses.
People freeze.
Someone says, is he all right?
In moments like this, the people who help are rarely the ones who know the most.
They're the ones who have a plan in their head.
This lesson gives you that plan.
We'll focus on the most serious situation, someone who has collapsed and isn't responding, because that's when a calm plan matters most.
It follows the current guidelines of the Australian Resuscitation Council, which are the basis of first aid training right across the country.
One important thing first.
This is a refresher, not a substitute for a proper first aid course.
CPR is a physical skill, and the best way to learn it is with your hands on a training manikin and an instructor watching.
If you haven't done a course, or it's been a while, please book one.
Many trainers suggest refreshing your CPR skills every year.
Courses are run by organisations like St John Ambulance and by many registered training providers, and a CPR course often takes only a few hours.
The plan has a name that's easy to remember.
DRSABCD.
It stands for Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR and Defibrillation.
One way to remember it is the phrase Doctors ABCD.
If you're driving, just listen along, and try saying the letters out loud with me.
D, R, S, A, B, C, D.
It's also worth knowing that you're protected.
Every Australian state and territory has laws that protect people who help in an emergency in good faith.
And when it comes to someone who isn't breathing, doing something is always better than doing nothing.
Part two. Danger to breathing.
D is for Danger.
Before you rush in, stop and look around.
Is there traffic, fire, electricity, deep water, or someone aggressive nearby?
You can't help anyone if you become a second casualty.
Only approach when it's safe for you, for bystanders, and for the person.
R is for Response.
Check whether the person responds.
First aid trainers often teach this with the word COWS.
Can you hear me?
Open your eyes.
What's your name?
Squeeze my hand.
Speak loudly and give their shoulders a firm squeeze.
If they don't respond at all, treat it as an emergency.
S is for Send for help.
Call triple zero, and ask for an ambulance.
If someone else is there, point at them and say, you, call triple zero, and come back to tell me.
A specific instruction to one person works far better than a general shout for help.
Put your phone on speaker so your hands are free.
The triple zero call taker will ask where you are and what's happened, and they can talk you through CPR step by step.
Don't hang up until they tell you to.
The free Emergency Plus app, developed with Australia's emergency services, can show your location if you're somewhere unfamiliar.
When you dial triple zero, the first voice you hear will ask whether you need police, fire or ambulance.
Say ambulance clearly, and you'll be connected.
Triple zero works from any phone, including a mobile with no credit.
If you're on your own, call first, put the phone on speaker beside you, and then carry on with the steps while you talk.
A is for Airway.
Open the person's mouth and check for anything blocking it, like vomit or food.
If you see something, roll them onto their side and clear it.
Then, with the person on their back, gently tilt the head back and lift the chin.
This lifts the tongue away from the back of the throat and opens the airway.
B is for Breathing.
Look, listen and feel for normal breathing, for no more than ten seconds.
Watch the chest, listen near the mouth, and feel for breath on your cheek.
Here's something important that catches many people out.
In the first minutes after the heart stops, a person may make occasional gasping sounds.
That is not normal breathing.
If breathing is absent or not normal, you need to start CPR.
If the person is unresponsive but breathing normally, roll them onto their side into the recovery position.
That helps keep the airway clear.
To do it, kneel beside them, place the arm nearest you out at a right angle, lay their other arm across their chest, bend their far knee up, and gently roll them towards you onto their side.
Tilt the head back slightly so fluids can drain from the mouth.
Keep watching their breathing until help arrives, and if it stops or stops being normal, roll them onto their back and start CPR.
Part three. CPR and defibrillation.
C is for CPR, which stands for cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
Kneel beside the person, who should be lying on their back on a firm surface.
Place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone, and put your other hand on top.
Keep your arms straight, and your shoulders over your hands.
Push down hard and fast.
For an adult, press down about one third of the depth of the chest.
Let the chest rise back up fully after each push.
The rate is one hundred to one hundred and twenty compressions a minute, which is about two every second.
Many people keep time to the beat of the song Stayin' Alive by the Bee Gees, which sits in that range.
The pattern is thirty compressions, then two rescue breaths.
Thirty to two.
For each breath, keep the head tilted and chin lifted, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs, and blow steadily until you see the chest rise.
Then go straight back to thirty compressions.
Aim for about five rounds of thirty to two every two minutes.
If you can't give breaths, or you're not willing to, that's okay.
Do compressions only, without stopping.
Continuous chest compressions can still save a life.
Don't worry about pressing too hard.
Ribs can crack during CPR, but without CPR, a person whose heart has stopped will die.
Children and babies need a slightly different technique, which is another good reason to do a hands-on course.
CPR is tiring, so if someone else is there, swap every two minutes, with as little pause as possible.
Keep going until the person starts to respond or breathe normally, until paramedics take over, or until you physically can't continue.
D is for Defibrillation.
An automated external defibrillator, often called an AED or a defib, is a portable device that can shock the heart back into a normal rhythm.
You'll see them in shopping centres, gyms, sports clubs, workplaces and airports.
Send someone to find one, but don't stop CPR yourself to go looking.
In many areas, the triple zero call taker can tell you where the nearest registered defib is.
It's worth noticing where the defibs are at your own workplace, gym or local shopping centre, before you ever need one.
You don't need training to use one.
Open the lid or press the button, and the machine talks you through every step.
It will tell you where to stick the pads on the bare chest.
It analyses the heart rhythm and only allows a shock if one is needed, so you can't accidentally shock someone who doesn't need it.
When it tells you, make sure nobody is touching the person.
Then follow the voice prompts and keep up CPR in between.
Every minute counts.
The sooner CPR and a defibrillator reach a person whose heart has stopped, the better their chance of surviving.
That's why ordinary bystanders make such a difference.
An ambulance can take many minutes to arrive, and you're already there.
Let's recap with the letters one more time.
Danger, Response, Send for help by calling triple zero, Airway, Breathing, CPR at thirty compressions to two breaths, and Defibrillation as soon as a defib arrives.
If you remember nothing else, remember this.
Call triple zero, push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, and get a defib.
And book a hands-on course to make it second nature.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does DRSABCD stand for?
Answer. Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR, Defibrillation.
Question two. What's the ratio of compressions to breaths in adult CPR?
Answer. Thirty compressions to two breaths.
Question three. Is occasional gasping a sign of normal breathing?
Answer. No. If breathing is absent or not normal, start CPR.
That's the end of First Aid Basics by Ear. You're better prepared already.
